extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of aesthetics, artists and creative writers, and readers of philosophical criticism on the sublime and beautiful
extracted.subtask_description: Philosophical and quasi-psychological criteria for what produces the beautiful and the sublime across the senses, aimed to guide understanding (and by extension the production) of aesthetic effects in art and nature. Emphasises sensory mechanics (touch, sight, hearing), associations, and physiological causes (tension, expectation, surprise).

rubrics_metrics.name: Smoothness and insensible variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Objects whose surface continually varies its direction, but never varies it suddenly, are pleasing; sudden changes, even of small magnitude, are disagreeable to feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and guidance: a quick warm or cold touch startles; a slight unexpected tap is disagreeable. Angular bodies (squares, triangles, abrupt outlines) afford little pleasure. This principle applies to touch and analogously to sight: smooth, gently curved, and gradually varying outlines are beautiful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Softness, warmth, and tactile pleasure as markers of beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Soft, smooth, variated, unangular bodies produce pleasurable states in touch and correlate with visual beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Touch contributes pleasures (softness, moderate warmth) that mirror visual pleasures (color, gradation). The text suggests that the same dispositions of surface and coloring that please the eye would, if color could be felt, please the touch as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color as a distinct visual pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Sight possesses the distinct advantage of color, which contributes to beauty in ways other senses cannot directly replicate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Color interacts with other visual qualities (smoothness, gradation) to produce beauty; its effects are discussed alongside tactile analogies but treated as a unique visual pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beautiful sounds: clearness, smoothness, and weakness
rubrics_metrics.description: The beautiful in music prefers clear, even, smooth, and weak sounds rather than loud, strong, shrill, harsh, or very deep tones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton's poetic description is invoked as an example ('linked sweetness long drawn out'). Great variety and quick transitions between measures/tones are contrary to the genius of the beautiful in music because they excite mirth or tumultuous passions rather than the 'melting, languor' characteristic of beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation of variety and avoidance of quick transitions for beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Great variety and rapid changes of measure or tone oppose the beautiful because they arouse sudden or tumultuous passions rather than the gentle, languid emotion associated with beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In both sight and hearing, slow gradation and continuity are preferred; rapid changes may be appropriate for mirth or excitement but not for producing the characteristic emotion of beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between the beautiful and the sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: The beautiful and the sublime are contrasted: beautiful objects are comparatively small, smooth, polished, light, delicate, and avoid strong right-line deviations; sublime objects are vast, rugged, negligent, dark, solid and massive, and may embrace strong right-line forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They are psychologically opposed (one founded on pleasure, the other on pain/terror) and should be kept distinct when intending to affect passions. When a predominant property is intended to affect the mind, accompanying properties should tend to the same effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficient causes are affections of mind/body producing aesthetic emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: To explain the cause of sublime and beautiful is to identify the affections of the mind that cause bodily changes, or the bodily properties that elicit determinate passions of the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author restricts 'cause' to proximate affections (e.g., tension of nerves, expectation) rather than ultimate metaphysical origins. This functional/physiological view supports design decisions that target particular emotional responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of association in aesthetic response
rubrics_metrics.description: Many aesthetic reactions arise from associations formed early in life, making it difficult to separate learned aversions or attractions from natural effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While association explains many idiosyncrasies, it cannot account for all responses; one should first seek natural properties producing effects before appealing to association. Associations can nevertheless modify or intensify natural responses (e.g., terror linked to darkness via stories).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pain and fear produce the bodily tension underlying the sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: Pain and fear act on the same bodily parts and in similar ways (unnatural tension, contractions, convulsive agitation), and terror (apprehension of pain or death) is a foundation capable of producing the sublime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physiological effects—teeth set, contracted brows, dilated eyes, hair standing on end, shrieks—are described to show how terror and pain generate intense bodily states that, when modulated, become sources of sublime emotion. This links aesthetic effect to bodily physiology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublime arises from modified terror/pain (delightful horror)
rubrics_metrics.description: A moderated form of pain or terror—one that exercises the body or finer organs without being actually noxious—can produce a mixed feeling: not positive pleasure but a 'delightful horror' or 'tranquillity tinged with terror' (sublime).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains why things that suggest danger at a safe remove (vastness, powerful sounds, etc.) can delight. Degrees of this emotion are named: astonishment (highest), then awe, reverence, respect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise/labor analogy: pain-like exertion yields positive effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical labor (a mode of pain) and a mode of terror serve as exercise for coarser and finer bodily/mental organs respectively; such exercise is necessary to maintain their vigor and can produce delight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because both coarse and fine faculties require tension to function well, art that produces controlled tension (akin to exercise) can yield satisfying, sublime effects. Overdoing the tension destroys faculties; moderation is key.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greatness of dimension produces sublimity via sensory strain
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual objects of very large dimension are sublime because they either (a) present many distinct points that cumulatively strain the retina, or (b) require rapid traversal of the eye so the ocular muscles and nerves are strained—both produce sensations akin to pain that underlie the sublime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a physiological account: very large uniform objects engage the eye in a way that approaches the verge of pain, producing grandeur. The same principle is applied to sound (repeated strokes) where repetition, expectation, and surprise build tension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and simplicity necessary to produce the greatest sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: A vast object must also be experienced as one simple, uninterrupted whole to sustain the attention and prevent relaxation; unity (simplicity and uniformity) is requisite to the experience of true grandeur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mind attends to one object at a time; multiple small distinct objects cannot substitute for a single, unified vast object. The uniformity prevents the attention from finding boundaries and gaining rest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artificial infinite: succession of uniform parts creates sublimity
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'artificial infinite'—a long, uniform succession of similar parts (e.g., a colonnade)—produces sublimity through repeated similar impulses that increase tension over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Auditory parallel: repeated similar strokes cause expectation and surprise that augment tension. Visual example: a colonnade seen in perspective causes successive similar impressions that compound into sublimity; repetition and uniformity are crucial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity of successive impressions is required
rubrics_metrics.description: For the cumulative tension that yields sublimity, successive vibrations or impressions must be similar; dissimilar successive impressions interrupt and dissipate the built-up effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pendulum analogy: repeated pushes in the same direction build a larger motion, but alternating directions prevent accumulation. In visual terms, alternating pillar shapes (round/square) prevent the sustained impression necessary for sublimity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition and detention (not mere vastness) produce the sublime over mere bigness
rubrics_metrics.description: A long bare wall is impressive for its vastness but lacks the repeated, detained impressions of a colonnade; sublimity depends on repetition and the eye being detained by successive similar ideas rather than on single vastness alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bare uniform surfaces can be grand, but they supply only one idea (vastness) rather than the repeated impulses that approach the verge of pain. Expectation and surprise from repetition are central to sublimity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation and surprise amplify aesthetic tension
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated strokes or sounds create expectation, and the arrival of the next stroke still produces surprise; the combination of stroke, expectation, and surprise increases tension and can bring sensation to the verge of pain, producing the sublime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: successive firing of cannon or returning strokes in music—each repetition augments bodily preparation and surprise, intensifying the effect beyond the mere physical stimulus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Darkness and blackness as natural causes of terror/sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: Darkness (and blackness) can be a natural source of terror and thus of the sublime because utter darkness deprives us of knowledge of surroundings and safety, engendering uncertainty and apprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues against Locke by asserting that darkness produces a general association of danger (we cannot know if we will strike an obstruction or be attacked). A clinical example (boy seeing black for first time) is offered to suggest a natural uneasiness before associative learning could operate.
